question: A consultant asks Claude to turn a dense technical whitepaper into a one-page executive brief, but the first attempt still restates most sentences from the whitepaper nearly verbatim. What refinement would best address this?
options: A) Ask Claude to identify decisions that matter most to executives and write fresh prose around them.
B) Ask Claude to keep the same original sentences but remove all adjectives and adverbs to save space.
C) Ask Claude to spread the whitepaper content across two pages instead of one so that nothing is cut.
D) Ask Claude to reduce the font size so the dense text still fits on one page despite its length.
correct_answers: A) Ask Claude to identify decisions that matter most to executives and write fresh prose around them.
explanations: Correct. This refinement directs Claude to synthesize the content around high-impact decisions, moving away from verbatim restatement. Writing fresh prose ensures the output is tailored to executive needs rather than a compressed copy of the original.

Incorrect. Stripping modifiers leaves the original sentence structures and verbatim phrasing intact, failing to synthesize the material into key takeaways. Executives require distilled insights, not trimmed versions of the same text.

Incorrect. Expanding to two pages avoids the need for synthesis and decision-making about what truly matters. An executive brief demands conciseness and focus, not simply more space for undifferentiated content.

Incorrect. Adjusting font size is a cosmetic change that does not address the underlying problem of undigested, sentence-by-sentence repetition. The content remains dense and unsuitable for an executive summary.
